query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a tailored nanohierarchical microstructure by inducing controlled in situ nanoprecipitation within the CoCrFeNi matrix will enable adaptive friction interface protection, thereby maintaining low friction and wear rates from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional equiatomic CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a relatively homogeneous microstructure and coarse grains lacking engineered nanoprecipitates.
generation.intervention: Apply a combined thermomechanical and thermal treatment protocol (or alloy design adjustment) to induce a nanohierarchical structure with nano‐coupled grains and finely dispersed secondary phase nanoprecipitates that create spatial composition undulations.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted in air (oxidative environment) under controlled load, spanning a temperature range from approximately 25 °C (room temperature) up to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence of an adaptive nanohierarchical architecture where the nanoscale precipitates at grain boundaries and within the grains act as stress relievers at low temperatures and promote the formation of a dense, nanocrystalline glaze layer at high temperatures.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the nanoprecipitates and nano‐coupled grains promote multiple deformation pathways to distribute frictional stress, while at elevated temperatures the engineered microstructure enables the formation of a protective glaze layer that minimizes adhesive and oxidative wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, the engineered variant is expected to exhibit a significantly reduced coefficient of friction and lower wear rates across the full temperature range; evidence in similar systems suggests improvements by up to an order of magnitude in wear resistance, though the exact quantitative change is uncertain.
generation.baseline: Performance data of standard CoCrFeNi alloys typically showing higher friction coefficients and wear rates, especially deteriorating at temperatures approaching 800 °C.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under sliding wear conditions in air with moderate to high contact loads between room temperature and 800 °C; extreme wear conditions or different environments (e.g., vacuum) may alter the mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: While similar nanostructuring strategies in other complex concentrated alloys (e.g., Ni50(AlNbTiV)50) have yielded ultra-low wear rates, the precise magnitude of improvement in the CoCrFeNi alloy remains to be verified and may depend on the uniformity and stability of the induced nanohierarchical features.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi alloy samples: one set processed via conventional methods (control) and another set subjected to the tailored thermomechanical and thermal treatment to induce the nanohierarchical microstructure. Conduct identical sliding wear experiments in air across the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under the same load conditions.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) at various temperatures
Wear rate (e.g., measured mass loss or wear volume per N·m)
Post-test microstructural analysis (SEM, TEM) to verify the presence and stability of the nanoprecipitates and glaze layer formation at high temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the treated CoCrFeNi samples do not exhibit a statistically significant lower friction coefficient and wear rate across the full temperature range compared to the control samples, or if the post-test microstructure fails to reveal the intended adaptive nanohierarchical features.

cited_evidence.text:
Remarkable Wear Resistance in a Complex Concentrated Alloy with Nanohierarchical Architecture and Composition Undulation

Abstract: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear.
